title: Sour Grapes: Each Person Answers to God
summary: The exiles are repeating a proverb that blames their suffering on their parents' sins. God forbids it: every life belongs to him, and each person will live or die by his own ways. Through three generations of test cases and a righteous man who falls and a wicked man who turns, the chapter ends in a plea: God takes no pleasure in anyone's death, so turn and live.
story: Ezekiel has spent seventeen chapters announcing that Jerusalem will fall and explaining why. The exiles in Babylon have heard him, and they have an answer ready: if judgment is coming, it is our fathers' fault, not ours. Chapter 18 takes that answer apart. It does not deny that one generation's sin shapes the next, a truth Ezekiel himself has laid out in the long history of chapter 16. It denies that the present generation is trapped by it. The chapter turns the book from fatalism toward responsibility and hope, and its closing call for a new heart and a new spirit looks ahead to the promise of chapter 36, where God himself gives what he here commands.
historical:
Ezekiel was a priest carried to Babylon in 597 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took King Jehoiachin and thousands of Jerusalem's leading citizens into exile (2 Kings 24:10-16). He lived among the deportees at a settlement by the Chebar canal and began to prophesy in 593 BC. Chapter 18 is undated, but it falls in the years before Jerusalem's destruction in 587 or 586 BC, when the exiles were trying to make sense of what had already happened to them and what they were told was still coming.

The proverb about sour grapes was not Ezekiel's invention. Jeremiah, preaching in Jerusalem in the same years, quotes it too and promises a day when it will no longer be said (Jeremiah 31:29-30). It was apparently common talk on both ends of the exile. The generation that saw the collapse had been told for decades that the sins of King Manasseh (about 697 to 642 BC) had sealed Judah's fate (2 Kings 21:10-15; 24:3-4), and it is easy to see how that teaching curdled into a slogan: the fathers sinned, we pay, and nothing we do matters.
cultural:
The portrait of the righteous man in verses 5 to 9 is a compact summary of Israel's law, the kind of checklist a priest like Ezekiel would know by heart. Eating at the mountain refers to sacrificial meals at hilltop shrines, the high places where Israel worshiped other gods or worshiped the LORD in forbidden ways. The sexual laws echo Leviticus 18 and 20. The economic laws come straight from the covenant code: a creditor who took a poor man's cloak as a pledge had to return it by sunset so he could sleep in it (Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-13), and Israelites were forbidden to charge interest to a fellow Israelite in need (Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20). In an agrarian economy where debt could end in slavery, these were not small rules.

What stands out is how much of the righteous life is about the poor: giving bread to the hungry, clothing the naked, refusing to profit from a neighbor's desperation. Worship, sexual faithfulness, and economic mercy sit side by side as one obedience. For Ezekiel, a man who kept the temple rules but squeezed his debtors was not righteous.
literary: The chapter is a disputation, a form Ezekiel uses often: he quotes what the people are saying (verse 2, and again in verses 19, 25, and 29), then answers it. The heart of the chapter is a three-generation case study in legal language, much like the case laws of the Torah (suppose a man, now suppose his son, now suppose that son has a son). Each case ends with a verdict: he will surely live, or he will surely die. Verses 21 to 29 add a second set of cases, the wicked man who turns and the righteous man who turns away, and the people's complaint that the LORD's way is not fair is thrown back at them twice. The word turn (shuv) runs through the second half and becomes the chapter's closing command.

outline.t: The sour-grapes proverb forbidden: every soul belongs to God
The grandson who refuses his father's ways lives
The son will not bear the father's iniquity
The wicked who turn live; the righteous who turn away die
Repent, make a new heart, and live

doctrines.note: The chapter is one of the Old Testament's fullest statements of repentance. A person's past, whether a father's sins or his own, does not decide his future before God; turning from sin to righteousness brings life, and the transgressions left behind will not be held against him (verse 22).

God judges each person according to his ways (verse 30). The chapter does not deny that communities suffer together or that sin has consequences across generations; it denies that anyone is condemned for a guilt that is not his own.
The chapter's deepest word is about God's heart: he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and would prefer that they turn and live (verses 23 and 32). His justice is real, but it is not eager.

words.note: Shuv, to turn or return, the Old Testament's main word for repentance. It is a word of direction rather than feeling: a person walking one way turns around and walks the other. It can describe the wicked turning to righteousness (verse 21) or the righteous turning away from it (verse 24), which is why the chapter can use it for both rescue and ruin.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. In Hebrew this is right relationship lived out in concrete acts: fair dealing, mercy to the poor, faithful worship. The chapter defines it by example rather than abstraction, which is typical of the Old Testament.

Takhan, to measure or weigh. The people's complaint in verses 25 and 29 is literally that the LORD's way is not measured right, as if God's scales were rigged. God answers that it is their scales that are off.

Nephesh, often translated soul, means the whole living person rather than an immaterial part. When verse 4 says the soul who sins will die, it means the person who sins, not someone else in his place.

christ: Ezekiel commands the exiles to make themselves a new heart and a new spirit (verse 31), and later the same book shows God promising to give exactly that: a new heart and his own Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:26-27). The command exposes the need; the promise meets it. The New Testament hears that promise fulfilled in the gift of the Spirit through Christ, and Jesus' words to Nicodemus about being born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5) have long been read against this background. The chapter's picture of God also carries into the New Testament: Peter writes that the Lord is patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9), and Paul says God desires all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). The chapter's principle that the one who sins will die sets the stage for the gospel's surprise, that Christ, who had no sin, died for sinners. That is a later development, not something Ezekiel foresaw in these words, but it answers the question his chapter leaves open: what happens to people who cannot make a new heart for themselves.

hard.q: Does this chapter contradict the Ten Commandments' warning that God visits the iniquity of fathers on children?
hard.a: Exodus 20:5 speaks of God visiting the iniquity of fathers on children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate him, while Ezekiel says a son will not bear his father's iniquity. Readers have handled the tension in several ways. Many note that the Exodus text itself limits the visitation to those who hate God, meaning children who continue their parents' sin, which is the very case of Ezekiel's violent son. Others point to Deuteronomy 24:16, which already forbade courts to execute children for their parents' crimes, and see Ezekiel applying that principle to God's own dealings. Still others see a real development within Scripture: Israel's older sense of corporate solidarity, in which families and nations stand or fall together, is balanced in the exile by a sharper emphasis on the individual. Most interpreters also note that Ezekiel is not writing a full theory of justice. He is answering a specific despair, and his point is pastoral: your parents' history does not close your door. The consequences of a nation's sin still fell on everyone in Jerusalem in 586 BC; what the chapter denies is that anyone stands condemned before God for a guilt that is not his own.

questions: What sour-grapes proverbs do people use today to explain why their lives cannot change? Which ones do you use?
The righteous man's life includes worship, sexual faithfulness, and generosity to the poor as a single obedience. Which of these do you tend to treat as optional?
God commands a new heart in verse 31 and promises to give one in chapter 36. How do you hold together the call to turn and the admission that we cannot remake ourselves?
